meta.title: Multi-tenant SaaS
meta.summary: One product serving thousands of customer organizations: shared pool for most tenants, dedicated silo for enterprise, strict isolation for all.

functional: Many customer organizations (tenants) use the same product
Each tenant only ever sees its own data
Enterprise tenants can get dedicated infrastructure
nonFunctional: No cross-tenant data leaks, even with an application bug
One noisy tenant cannot slow down others
Onboard a new tenant in minutes

scale.label: Daily active users
scale.value: 1M across all tenants, ~20 writes each per day

scale.label: API requests
scale.value: ~2,500/s average, ~10,000/s at weekday peak (4x), 10 reads per write

slos.name: API availability, per tenant
slos.sli: Requests not answered with a 5xx, divided by all requests, measured at the gateway per tenant so a large tenant cannot hide a small one's outage. A 429 from the tenant's own limit counts as good.

slos.name: API speed, per tenant
slos.sli: Requests answered within the threshold, divided by all requests, measured at the gateway per tenant, so one tenant slowing the pool shows up on its neighbours

slos.name: Tenant isolation
slos.sli: Responses whose records all carry the caller's tenant id. Detective, not preventive: checked on every response by the app's tenant guard (tenant_mismatch_total) and offline on a daily sample of logged responses. Row-level security and the signed context are what prevent leaks; this measures whether they held.

slos.name: Background jobs start on time
slos.sli: Jobs that start within the threshold of being queued, divided by all jobs, measured by the workers. Time a job waits because its own tenant is at its 2-job cap does not count against it.

alerts.when: tenant_mismatch_total above zero: the app's tenant guard saw a record, cache entry or job whose tenant id differs from the signed context
alerts.why: A data leak is the worst failure this product can have. The guard blocks that response, so the counter is the real-time signal; the daily sampled audit catches leaks the guard cannot see.

alerts.when: API errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
API errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak, often one tenant's errors, that would use up the month's budget before anyone is paged.

alerts.when: Requests over 300 ms burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Slow responses hurt every tenant at once when they come from shared infrastructure.

alerts.when: Requests over 300 ms burning the latency budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: Gradual slowdown, typically a pooled database growing into its limits or a tenant outgrowing the pool.

alerts.when: Jobs starting late burning the job-start budget 6 times too fast (checked over 30 minutes and 6 hours)
alerts.why: Pooled workers are not keeping up; scale them out before tenants notice. Background work is not urgent enough to page.

alerts.when: One tenant above 50% of the pooled database's total query time for 15 minutes (summed per tenant by the app, since the database cannot split CPU by tenant)
alerts.why: A noisy neighbour that its statement timeout and connection cap are not containing. Tighten its plan limits or move it to its own silo.

alerts.when: Pooled database connections above 80% of the maximum, or writer CPU above 75%, for 15 minutes
alerts.why: At peak the App Service can open up to 480 connections; running out turns into errors for every pooled tenant at once.

alerts.when: Any message in either dead-letter queue
alerts.why: A job failed 5 times and stopped retrying; some tenant is waiting for an export or bulk job that will never finish on its own.

alerts.when: A tenant receiving 429 responses for over 30 minutes, or using over 80% of its plan's rate limit at peak
alerts.why: Either an abusive client or a limit set too low for their plan.

alerts.when: Authentication or context-signature failures above 3 times the baseline for 10 minutes, or the context-signing key within 14 days of expiry
alerts.why: Could be an expired or rotated signing key, a misconfigured tenant or an attack.

signals.name: Requests, errors and 429s per tenant
signals.why: Slicing by tenant finds the one customer who is hurting or being hurt. 10,000 tenants is fine as a label; per-user would not be.

signals.name: Query time for the top 10 tenants
signals.why: Finds noisy neighbours before the whole pool is slow.

signals.name: Database connections in use, per tenant
signals.why: Shows the per-tenant cap of 5 connections doing its job, and which tenant holds the pool when it is full.

signals.name: Tenant context mismatches
signals.why: Should always be zero: before a response, cache write or job is sent, the guard checks every record's tenant id against the signed context.

signals.name: Jobs waiting per tenant, and oldest job age
signals.why: Shows a tenant held back by its concurrency cap, and whether the pooled workers keep up overall.

signals.name: Tenant onboarding time
signals.why: The business promise of onboarding in minutes, measured from sign-up to the catalog entry being ready.

signals.name: Active tenants and requests by plan
signals.why: Business view: usage per plan shows which tenants are close to an upgrade or to a silo.

steps: Filter every dashboard by that tenant id.
Compare with the pool: is the whole pool slow or only this tenant?
Look for a heavy query or export from another tenant using the same database.
Consider moving the heavy tenant to its own silo.
Take the trace id from the blocked response's log line and follow it from the gateway through the App Service.
Compare the signed context's tenant with the tenant of the record that failed the guard: a cache key, a job message or a query.
If a cache key lacked the tenant prefix, flush the affected keys; if a query ran without SET LOCAL, find the code path that took a connection outside a transaction.
Check the sampled audit for the same window to see whether any response got past the guard, and start the incident process if so.

debug.symptom: A tenant says its export or bulk job never finished
steps: Look up the job row by id: still queued, running or failed.
If queued, check jobs_waiting for that tenant: it may simply be behind its own 2-job cap.
If running for long, check the slot lease: an expired lease means the worker died and the job will be retried.
If failed, read the message in the dead-letter queue, fix the cause and send it back to the main queue.

nodes.label: Tenant user
nodes.description: Browser on the tenant's own subdomain, e.g. globex.app.com

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Rule set attached to the CDN: managed rules, IP rate rules, bot control

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Caches static assets only; /api/* is never cached

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.description: Verifies tokens, resolves the tenant, applies per-tenant limits, signs the tenant context (tenant, database, limits) with a key from the secrets manager

nodes.label: Identity Provider
nodes.description: OIDC; tokens carry a tenant_id claim (in Cognito a custom: attribute in the ID token, or a claim added to the access token by a pre token generation trigger)

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer
nodes.description: Private; reached by the gateway over a VPC Link; health-checks the App Service instances

nodes.label: App Service
nodes.description: Shared, stateless, 6 to 24 instances; takes tenant and database only from the gateway's signed context, never from the client

nodes.label: Tenant Catalog
nodes.description: tenant → plan, tier (pool / silo), database, limits

nodes.label: Pooled Cache
nodes.description: Keys prefixed with tenant id; ~50 GB

nodes.label: Pooled DB
nodes.description: All small tenants; every table has tenant_id with forced row-level security; writer plus a standby replica in another zone

nodes.label: Acme Dedicated DB
nodes.description: One enterprise tenant; own encryption key

nodes.label: Acme Job Queue
nodes.description: Only Acme's jobs; own dead-letter queue

nodes.label: Pooled Job Queue
nodes.description: Shared by all pooled tenants; messages carry tenant id; dead-letter queue after 5 failed attempts

nodes.label: Pooled Workers
nodes.description: Shared background capacity; at most 2 running jobs per tenant

flows.title: Request from a pooled tenant
flows.summary: The tenant comes from the verified token, its limits and database from the catalog via a context the gateway signs, and the database itself enforces isolation.

steps.label: resolve globex.app.com
steps.detail: A wildcard record sends every tenant subdomain to the same entry point.

steps.label: GET /api/projects
steps.detail: The tenant's subdomain and token travel together; the token is what counts.
steps.payload:
GET /api/projects HTTP/2
Host: globex.app.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…  (claims: sub=u_17, tenant_id=globex)

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: The CDN runs the attached WAF rules before forwarding: managed rule sets (SQL injection, known bad inputs), a per-IP rate rule and bot control. A blocked request gets a 403 at the edge and never reaches the gateway.

steps.label: forward, not cached
steps.detail: Caching is off for /api/* (the origin also sends Cache-Control: private, no-store) because every answer is tenant-specific, so one tenant's response can never be served to another. The CDN only terminates TLS near the user.

steps.label: verify JWT
steps.detail: Usually a local signature check with cached public keys. The tenant comes from the signed token, never from a header or body field the client controls.

steps.label: valid, tenant=globex
steps.detail: The gateway also checks the token's tenant matches the subdomain.

steps.label: GET tenant globex
steps.detail: Cached at the gateway for 60 s. That staleness only matters while a tenant changes database, and the migration fences the old copy so a stale entry fails safely (see the catalog note).

steps.label: per-tenant rate limit
steps.detail: Protects request rate only: a tenant over its limit gets 429s. Query cost is capped further down, by the statement timeout and connection cap the gateway passes on in the context.

steps.label: + signed tenant context
steps.detail: Sent over a VPC Link (private integration) to the internal load balancer. The gateway adds a short-lived context it signs itself, carrying the tenant, its database and its limits, so no service ever uses a client-supplied value or needs its own catalog lookup. A W3C traceparent header starts here and travels on every later hop, including job messages.
steps.payload:
GET /api/projects
X-Tenant-Context: tenant=globex; tier=pool; db=pool-1; stmt_timeout_ms=2000; db_conn_cap=5; exp=1731400030; sig=…
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

steps.label: to a healthy instance
steps.detail: The managed gateway scales itself, but the 6 to 24 App Service instances still need balancing and health checks: the load balancer only sends to instances passing them, across all three zones.

steps.label: verify context, pick pool-1
steps.detail: Checks the gateway's signature and expiry, then takes a connection from the pool named by db=pool-1. The routing came with the request, so the App Service never calls the catalog.

steps.label: GET globex:projects
steps.detail: Every cache key is prefixed with the tenant id from the signed context.

steps.label: SELECT with RLS
steps.detail: Row-level security: even if a query forgets WHERE tenant_id = …, the database only returns this tenant's rows. It holds because the app connects as a role that does not own the tables and has no BYPASSRLS, the tables use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and the tenant is set with SET LOCAL so it ends with the transaction; with no tenant set the policy matches nothing. One tenant may use at most 5 of an instance's 20 connections to this database.

steps.label: tenant guard
steps.detail: Before responding, the app checks every record's tenant_id against the signed context; a mismatch blocks the response and increments tenant_mismatch_total. Row-level security prevents leaks; this guard detects one if a bug gets past it.

flows.title: Request from an enterprise tenant
flows.summary: Same code path; the catalog entry, carried in the signed context, routes Acme to its dedicated database, queue and workers.

steps.label: POST /api/exports
steps.payload:
POST /api/exports HTTP/2
Host: acme.app.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…  (claims: tenant_id=acme)
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2e
steps.detail: The client sends an idempotency key, so a retried POST cannot start the same export twice.

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: Same WAF rules for every tenant, before the request costs any gateway capacity.

steps.label: + signed tenant context
steps.detail: The catalog entry travels in the signed context, so the routing decision is made once, at the gateway.
steps.payload:
POST /api/exports
X-Tenant-Context: tenant=acme; tier=silo; db=acme-db; exp=1731400030; sig=…
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

steps.label: INSERT export job
steps.detail: Connection chosen from db=acme-db in the signed context, not from a catalog call. The app code is identical for pooled and siloed tenants. A unique (tenant_id, idempotency_key) on the jobs table turns a retry into a lookup of the existing job.

steps.label: enqueue (tenant=acme)
steps.detail: tier=silo in the context selects Acme's own queue, so its exports never wait behind pooled tenants' jobs.

steps.label: job_9
steps.detail: Acme's heavy exports run on Acme's own workers, so they never compete with pooled tenants.

flows.title: A pooled tenant starts a huge bulk job
flows.summary: Rate limits do not help here: one request starts hours of work. Pooled workers cap each tenant at 2 running jobs, and short transactions with a statement timeout cap what each query can cost.

steps.label: POST bulk archive
steps.detail: One small request that starts work on two million rows.
steps.payload:
POST /api/projects/bulk-archive HTTP/2
Host: globex.app.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…  (claims: tenant_id=globex)
Idempotency-Key: 9b77d0

{ "updated_before": "2024-01-01" }

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: Nothing to block: it is a valid request from a real user.

steps.label: token, catalog, rate limit
steps.detail: The same checks as any request. One request is far under 100 requests/s, which is why rate limits alone cannot stop this kind of load.

steps.label: INSERT job row
steps.detail: Recorded under row-level security like any other write, so the job belongs to globex. The unique (tenant_id, idempotency_key) makes a retried POST return the same job.

steps.label: enqueue (tenant=globex)
steps.detail: Pooled tenants share one queue and one worker fleet; fairness comes from the per-tenant cap the workers enforce. The 202 is only sent after this enqueue, so if the app dies in between, the client retries with the same idempotency key and the app finds the queued job and enqueues it again. Delivery is at least once, so every job must be safe to run twice; this one is, since each batch only touches rows not yet archived.

steps.label: job_77 (tenant=globex)
steps.detail: Any pooled worker can take any tenant's job.

steps.label: take 1 of globex's 2 slots
steps.detail: Each tenant has two slot rows with leases. Row locks with SKIP LOCKED let concurrent workers each take a different free slot, and a crashed worker's lease simply expires. If no slot is free, the worker lets the message reappear after a delay and takes another tenant's job, so globex can queue 50 jobs but only ever runs 2.
steps.payload:
UPDATE job_slots SET job_id = 'job_77', lease_until = now() + interval '5 minutes'
WHERE (tenant_id, slot_no) = (
  SELECT tenant_id, slot_no FROM job_slots
  WHERE tenant_id = 'globex' AND lease_until < now()
  LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING slot_no;   -- no row back: globex is at its cap

steps.label: archive 1,000 rows, commit, repeat
steps.detail: Each batch is its own short transaction with the tenant and statement timeout set, so no statement holds locks or a connection for long and other tenants' queries get connections between batches. The worker renews its lease as it goes and frees the slot at the end.

notes.text: Pool (shared everything) is cheapest and easiest to operate. Silo (dedicated per tenant) gives the strongest isolation and per-tenant tuning at higher cost, and allows customer-managed encryption keys and a dedicated network for compliance. Most products pool by default and silo enterprise customers.

Defense in depth: tenant from the signed token, passed on in a gateway-signed context, and row-level security in the database, so one forgotten WHERE clause cannot leak data. RLS only holds if the app's role does not own the tables and lacks BYPASSRLS, the tables use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and the tenant is set with SET LOCAL per transaction: a session-level SET would stay on the pooled connection for the next tenant's request. Two gaps remain: foreign key and unique checks bypass row security (so a duplicate key error can reveal that another tenant's row exists, which composite keys that start with tenant_id avoid), and a view runs with its owner's rights unless it is created with security_invoker.

Because routing comes from the catalog, a tenant that outgrows the pool can move to its own database: copy, stream changes, then cut over. Gateways cache entries for 60 s, so the cutover first fences the old copy (the tenant is marked moved in the pool and the write policy rejects its writes), then flips the entry. For up to one TTL a stale gateway still routes there and gets a retryable error rather than writing to the old copy. When one pooled database runs hot, add pool-2 for new tenants; the catalog's db field already allows it.

Noisy neighbours are contained at three levels: request rate per tenant at the gateway; query cost in the pooled database (a statement timeout and at most 5 of each instance's 20 connections, both from the plan in the signed context); and background work, at most 2 running jobs per tenant on the pooled workers. Silo tenants get their own queue and workers instead.

Each database is a writer with a standby replica in another zone. If the writer fails or its zone is lost, the managed service promotes the replica, usually within a minute; writes fail meanwhile, and the app reconnects through the cluster endpoint and retries only idempotent requests. The App Service runs in all three zones, so losing one leaves two thirds of it while autoscaling refills the rest. At peak, 24 instances with 20 connections each is up to 480 connections to the pooled writer, which sizes the database or calls for a connection proxy in front.

The WAF on the CDN drops common attacks and floods before they cost gateway capacity, using managed rule sets, per-IP rate rules and bot control. It cannot replace the per-tenant limits at the gateway, which need the verified tenant. The CDN caches only static assets; /api/* is never cached, since every response belongs to one tenant.

Data stores sit in the private data subnet, reachable only from the app subnet. The managed pieces outside the VPC (queues, catalog, key service) are reached through VPC endpoints, so tenant data never crosses the internet. Silo databases are encrypted with the customer's own key in the cloud key service (AWS KMS / Cloud KMS), used by the database service itself, so no request path calls it; the gateway's context-signing key lives in the secrets manager and is rotated with an overlap window.

questions.q: One tenant runs a huge import and slows down everyone in the pool. How do you prevent that?
questions.a: Rate limits alone do not help, since one request can start hours of work. Run the import on the pooled workers with at most 2 running jobs per tenant, in short batches, and give every pooled transaction a per-tenant statement timeout and connection cap from its plan. Watch query time per tenant, and move tenants who consistently need more to a dedicated tier.

questions.q: In the pooled database, how do you make sure a bug never shows one tenant another tenant's data?
questions.a: Every table carries a tenant id, and the database enforces it with row-level security bound to the tenant from the signed context: set with SET LOCAL in each transaction so a pooled connection never carries it over, under a role that does not own the tables, with RLS forced. Cache keys and job messages carry the tenant id too. Detect what slips through with the app's tenant guard (a mismatch counter that should stay at zero), cross-tenant tests and sampled audits.

questions.q: How does a request find the right database for its tenant?
questions.a: The gateway takes the tenant from the verified token, checks it against the hostname, and looks it up in the catalog, which maps it to its tier and database. It caches entries for 60 s and puts the database id into the context it signs, so the App Service picks its connection pool without a catalog call of its own. Moving a tenant updates the catalog, not the code.

questions.q: A pooled tenant upgrades to the enterprise tier. How do you move them to a dedicated database without downtime?
questions.a: Copy their rows to the new database, then stream ongoing changes until it catches up. Fence the old copy so it rejects that tenant's writes, let the last changes arrive, verify, and flip the catalog entry. Gateways may still route to the old copy for up to the 60 s cache TTL, where writes fail with a retryable error instead of landing in the wrong place, so the tenant sees about a minute of retries. Keep the old copy until you are confident, then delete it.

questions.q: How do you know which tenants are affected during an incident?
questions.a: Tag every metric, log and trace with the tenant id and tier, so you can break down errors and latency per tenant. Per-tenant SLOs show whether the enterprise tenants are within their contract. Watch label cardinality: tag by tenant, not by user.

questions.q: How do you roll out a schema change across one pooled database and many dedicated ones?
questions.a: Use backward-compatible, expand-and-contract migrations: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old one later. Roll it through dedicated databases in waves with automation and tracking, since each is its own deployment.
